name: Archaeological Site Conservation
description: Archaeological conservation protects the physical remains, records, and settings through which Iran’s past can be studied. Persepolis and Bam illustrate different challenges: safeguarding monumental ruins against development pressures and conserving an earthen settlement within a living oasis.

seo.title: Archaeological Site Conservation in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore archaeological conservation in Iran through Persepolis, Bam, and the principles governing excavation, maintenance, authenticity, and setting.

content.heading: Protecting evidence, including what remains underground
content.content:
An archaeological site is more than a collection of objects or impressive walls. Its value also lies in the relationships among remains, their original locations, and the records produced when they are investigated. The archaeological heritage charter adopted by the International Council on Monuments and Sites, or ICOMOS, treats protection as a continuing responsibility involving researchers, public authorities, other specialists, and communities. [s1](https://icomosjapan.org/static/homepage/charter/charter1990.pdf)

This approach makes excavation a consequential decision. The charter recommends leaving part of an investigated site undisturbed for future research and making excavation reports available to the scholarly community. Its conservation principle is preservation in situ: keeping heritage in its original context. It also cautions against exposing remains when their subsequent maintenance cannot be assured. These are professional standards, rather than evidence that every Iranian excavation follows them. [s1]

content.heading: Persepolis: protecting ruins and their surroundings
content.content:
At Persepolis, the Achaemenid royal complex in southwestern Iran, conservation concerns both surviving monuments and the land around them. UNESCO identifies agricultural expansion, construction, industrial development, and the growth of nearby settlements as pressures on the property and its buffer zone. A buffer zone helps protect the surroundings that contribute to a heritage property’s significance; it is not simply unused land awaiting development. [s2](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/114/)

UNESCO’s statement describes restoration using traditional materials and technology while respecting the ensemble’s authenticity. It identifies the Persepolis Research Base as responsible for investigation, conservation, restoration, organization, and presentation. Its management requirements also call for monitoring pollutants, weathering, and other environmental factors. These requirements establish what needs sustained attention; the listing statement alone does not demonstrate that every monitoring measure is operating effectively today. [s2]

content.heading: Bam: earthen architecture within an oasis
content.content:
Bam presents a different conservation problem. Its fortified settlement uses layered earth and sun-dried mud brick, while the surrounding oasis depends historically on qanats, underground channels that convey water. UNESCO treats the settlement, hydraulic systems, agricultural land, and their relationships as a cultural landscape. Conserving the citadel therefore cannot be separated completely from conserving its setting. [s3](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1208/)

The 2003 earthquake damaged the citadel, including sections of its defensive walls and governor’s quarters. UNESCO’s conservation statement emphasizes original materials, traditional techniques, and the reliability of documentary and field evidence when considering restoration or partial reconstruction. The distinction matters: a convincing new surface does not by itself establish historical accuracy. [s3]

content.heading: How to assess conservation claims
content.content: These examples suggest useful questions when reading about an Iranian archaeological project. What evidence supports the intervention? How will exposed remains be maintained? Does protection extend to the surrounding landscape? Are published management requirements being mistaken for completed work? The answers help distinguish a documented conservation approach from an attractive presentation of ruins. Conservation succeeds over time through continued care, research, and protection of context. [s1][s2][s3]

name: Sustainable Tourism Management
description: Sustainable tourism management connects heritage protection, residents’ interests, visitor behavior, and local economic benefits. In Iran’s historic destinations, it provides a framework for assessing tourism development without assuming that higher visitor numbers automatically mean better outcomes.

seo.title: Sustainable Tourism Management in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand how heritage destinations can manage visitors, involve residents, distribute local benefits, and measure conservation outcomes.

content.heading: What sustainable management involves
content.content:
Sustainable tourism is a management responsibility encompassing the destination, its heritage, and the people who live there. UNESCO’s World Heritage tourism toolkit connects strategy and governance with community engagement, infrastructure, visitor behavior, investment, and monitoring. Its guidance is intended to help destinations choose measures suited to their circumstances. It does not certify that a destination has become sustainable simply because it has adopted a plan. [s1](https://whc.unesco.org/en/sustainabletourismtoolkit/)

For readers exploring Iran, this distinction helps make sense of claims about heritage hotels, restored neighborhoods, and tourism growth. The relevant questions concern what is protected, who benefits, and what evidence shows that management is working. The toolkit offers a framework for asking those questions rather than a single formula applicable everywhere. [s1]

content.heading: Residents are participants in the destination
content.content:
UNESCO’s community-engagement guide emphasizes continuing dialogue with residents and local businesses. It recommends identifying both benefits and harms, incorporating realistic community priorities into strategy, and monitoring whether a place remains livable. Access to heritage can also matter to local cultural life independently of tourism. [s2](https://whc.unesco.org/en/sustainabletourismtoolkit/guide4)

Economic benefits require deliberate choices. The guide identifies opportunities in accommodation, food, transport, retail, and interpretation, while warning that changes can disadvantage existing livelihoods. Replacing transport arrangements, for example, can affect the people already providing those services. Local participation therefore concerns decisions and access to opportunity as well as employment totals. These are recommended practices, not verified findings about their implementation across Iran. [s2]

content.heading: Yazd: tourism within a living historic city
content.content:
Yazd illustrates why management must consider more than individual attractions. UNESCO describes a historic city whose earthen buildings, shaded alleys, courtyards, wind-catchers, and qanat water systems form an interconnected response to desert conditions. The heritage includes inhabited neighborhoods and social traditions, alongside monumental architecture. [s3](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1544/)

The listing statement records hotels and restaurants operating in rehabilitated historic buildings, with physical elements retained and interventions minimized. It also describes coordination among heritage authorities, the municipality, communities, and waqf institutions—endowments associated with public and religious facilities. These examples show the range of interests involved in adaptive reuse. They do not establish the present distribution of tourism income or demonstrate that every conversion benefits residents. [s3]

content.heading: Manage pressure where and when it occurs
content.content:
An annual visitor total can conceal crowding at particular entrances, streets, or times. UNESCO’s visitor-management guidance recommends examining seasonal, daily, and hourly patterns using ticket records, observation, and the knowledge of people working at the destination. It cautions against treating carrying capacity as one permanently valid number: acceptable pressure depends on the heritage, conditions, and community impacts. [s4](https://whc.unesco.org/en/sustainabletourismtoolkit/guide8)

For an Iranian destination, this means a proposal to disperse visitors or restrict access should be assessed against evidence about the actual pressure. The guidance also recognizes that sensitive heritage may require forms of interpretation that do not involve direct physical access. These are management options, not claims that a particular Iranian site currently applies them. [s4]

content.heading: Measure outcomes and adjust
content.content:
UNESCO’s monitoring guide groups evidence around conservation, community impacts, and tourism performance. It recommends site-specific benchmarks and repeatable observations so that managers can distinguish improvement from deterioration. Residents should help shape the questions used to evaluate effects on their lives. [s5](https://whc.unesco.org/en/sustainabletourismtoolkit/guide10)

For Iran, a credible sustainability account would therefore connect tourism activity to documented heritage condition and local outcomes. Announcing investment or recording more admissions establishes neither result on its own. Transparent monitoring makes it possible to revise management when benefits fall short or pressures increase. [s5]

content.title: A tourism-management learning cycle
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Understand heritage and tourism pressures"] -->|"Inform discussion"| B["Listen to residents and local businesses"]
  B -->|"Shape priorities"| C["Agree objectives and responsibilities"]
  C -->|"Guide action"| D["Manage services and visitor behavior"]
  D -->|"Generate evidence"| E["Monitor heritage and community outcomes"]
  E -->|"Revise understanding"| A
```
content.summary: This editorial synthesis connects UNESCO’s guidance into a feedback cycle. It describes a recommended approach, rather than an administrative process verified at every Iranian destination.

name: Political Institutions & Governance
description: Iran’s political system combines elected institutions with clerical oversight and extensive authority vested in the Supreme Leader. Understanding governance requires separating constitutional responsibilities from the ways candidate screening, security institutions, and competing centers of influence shape political practice.

seo.title: Iran’s Political Institutions & Governance | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: An introduction to Iran’s constitutional structure, elected offices, clerical oversight, security institutions, local government, and political practice.

content.heading: A republic organized around clerical guardianship
content.content:
Iran’s institutional system emerged from the revolution that ended the Pahlavi monarchy in 1979. Its constitution established an Islamic republic and was substantially revised in 1989. The system combines representative institutions with velayat-e faqih, usually translated as guardianship of the Islamic jurist: a doctrine that places a qualified religious jurist at the apex of political authority. Historian Saïd Amir Arjomand’s account emphasizes that this arrangement emerged through argument and institutional struggle, rather than expressing an uncontested religious blueprint. [s1](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/constitution-of-the-islamic-republic/)

This history helps explain why Iran’s government cannot be understood solely through the familiar division into executive, legislature, and judiciary. Those institutions exist, but operate within a wider structure of clerical supervision. The relationship between popular representation and religious authority is built into the system’s constitutional design. Readers should distinguish that design from judgments about how effectively institutions represent the population or constrain power in practice. [s1][s2]

content.heading: Leadership and the elected executive
content.content:
The constitution gives the Supreme Leader authority over general state policy and supreme command of the armed forces, together with important appointment powers. It separately identifies the president as head of the executive except in matters reserved for the leadership. These provisions explain why winning a presidential election does not confer control over every major instrument of the state. [s2](https://www.constituteproject.org/constitution/Iran_1989?lang=en)

The presidency nevertheless matters. It leads government administration, while the cabinet and ministries handle major areas of public policy. The House of Commons Library’s country profile distinguishes the president’s role as head of government from the Supreme Leader’s position as head of state. It also notes the constitutional role of the Assembly of Experts in selecting, supervising, and potentially dismissing the leader, while emphasizing the limited visibility of its supervisory proceedings. Formal accountability should therefore be distinguished from publicly demonstrable scrutiny. [s3](https://researchbriefings.files.parliament.uk/documents/CBP-10588/CBP-10588.pdf)

content.heading: Parliament, legislative review, and electoral boundaries
content.content:
The Majles, Iran’s parliament, is a central institution of lawmaking, but parliamentary approval is only part of the legislative process. The Guardian Council examines legislation for compatibility with Islamic criteria and the constitution. Its composition connects several institutions: the Supreme Leader appoints its religious jurists, while parliament selects its legal specialists from nominees presented by the judiciary’s head. [s4](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/guardian-council/)

The council also has constitutional interpretation and election-supervision functions. Encyclopaedia Iranica’s institutional account explains how these powers make it a major political gatekeeper. Disagreements between parliament and the Guardian Council can reach the Expediency Council, an institution incorporated into the revised constitutional structure. These relationships mean that legislative authority is distributed across bodies with different methods of selection and different claims to legitimacy. [s4]

Candidate screening also shapes the choices offered to voters. The Commons Library describes the exclusion of many candidates outside the leadership-aligned establishment. Elections should consequently be examined through eligibility rules and implementation as well as voting procedures. An elected office can carry substantial responsibilities while the competition for that office remains restricted. [s3]

content.heading: Security policy and overlapping centers of influence
content.content:
Security governance brings together elected officials, military leaders, and representatives of the Supreme Leader. The Council on Foreign Relations describes the Supreme National Security Council as a forum including the president, other branch heads, ministers, military chiefs, and leadership representatives. Its remit covers major defense and security questions. The institution illustrates how participation by an elected official can coexist with other sources of authority inside the same decision-making body. [s5](https://www.cfr.org/articles/islamic-republics-power-centers)

An organizational chart remains incomplete without attention to political influence. CFR’s account describes republican institutions embedded within clerical structures and emphasizes multiple centers of power. The practical question is often which actors can shape appointments, block proposals, or mobilize resources in a particular policy area. That answer may differ between economic administration, security, and foreign relations; a single hierarchy cannot capture every interaction. [s5]

content.heading: The documented leadership transition in 2026
content.content:
The distinction between procedure and influence became especially significant during the 2026 succession. Reuters reported in March that the Assembly of Experts selected Mojtaba Khamenei following the death of his father, Ali Khamenei, in the opening phase of the United States–Israeli attacks. The Commons Library’s March profile also records the succession. It should not be described as an automatic hereditary transfer: the formal selection mechanism remained the Assembly. [s3][s6](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/irans-new-leader-still-silent-was-elevated-by-the-revolutionary-guards-4553207)

Reuters separately reported, citing senior Iranian sources and insiders, that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps exerted decisive pressure in favor of the selection. That account concerns reported political influence, rather than a constitutional power assigning the Guards the choice of leader. Its source-based character matters: it provides evidence about a partly opaque process without making every private interaction independently observable. [s6]

content.heading: Government beyond the national leadership
content.content:
Governance also encompasses public administration and local affairs. The constitution provides for elected councils at local and provincial levels and recognizes government-appointed territorial officials. Local participation therefore exists within a centrally organized state, rather than constituting a separate sovereign tier. Constitutional provisions establish responsibilities; evaluating actual autonomy requires examining the relevant laws, resources, and administrative practice. [s2]

The branches of this guide separate government structure, legislative and executive institutions, the judiciary, urban and provincial administration, and elections. Other branches examine political currents, public policy, foreign relations, international organizations, digital governance, civil society, and transparency. Together, they support a practical way of reading Iranian governance: identify the institution, establish its formal authority, then examine evidence about how that authority is exercised. The 2026 succession demonstrates why both steps remain necessary. [s2][s6]

content.title: Selected constitutional appointment and review relationships
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  E["Assembly of Experts"] -->|"Selects"| L["Supreme Leader"]
  L -->|"Appoints judiciary head"| J["Head of Judiciary"]
  L -->|"Appoints religious jurists"| G["Guardian Council"]
  J -->|"Nominates legal specialists"| N["Legal specialist nominees"]
  N -->|"Considered for selection by"| P["Parliament"]
  P -->|"Selects legal specialists"| G
  P -->|"Submits legislation for review"| G
  G -->|"Reviews compatibility with Islam and constitution"| B["Parliamentary legislation"]
```
content.summary: The arrows identify distinct selection, nomination, and legislative-review functions. This is a partial constitutional map; it does not quantify influence or depict all institutions and accountability mechanisms.

limitations: This overview distinguishes constitutional powers from scholarly interpretation and attributed reporting about political practice.
Historical scholarly references explain institutional development and are not treated as current officeholder directories.
The 2026 succession account is supported by March reporting and a parliamentary briefing; this page does not establish every subsequent appointment or operational change through October.
The constitutional diagram is selective and does not imply that formal appointment relationships fully explain political influence.
data_gaps: No coherent annual numerical indicator directly represents this broad institutional category. Institutional powers have not been assigned artificial scores.
Comparable annual election, administrative-performance, and public-opinion series were not established for this overview.
